Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) --     More than 5,000 patients of a South Dakota urology clinic may have been exposed to hepatitis and HIV when the facility reused single-use medical products, state health officials said Friday. Clinic workers told inspectors they've been reusing products since the clinic opened its doors in 2002. The Siouxland Urology Center in Dakota Dunes has been ordered to contact nearly 5,700 former patients treated there since 2002. A routine inspection found the facility was reusing sterile saline bags, tubing and other medical supplies from cystoscopies -- a diagnostic procedure that looks at the lower urinary tract. "We witnessed the practice while we were in the facility," during a January inspection, said Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Health Department. Siouxland Urology has since been put under a provisional license and has been very cooperative, according to state officials. "Siouxland Urology Center informed certain of its patients by U.S. mail that a prior cystoscopy procedure could have potentially exposed them to an infectious disease," the facility's Web site said. It added that "the risk of infection from our past procedure is very minimal and we are unaware of any blood infections in our patients caused by the cystoscopy practice." The clinic, which primarily serves clients from South Dakota, Iowa and Nebraska, is offering free blood tests to those possibly affected to rule out the presence of viruses .Watch more on the possible exposure of urology patients » . On January 21, South Dakota Department of Health inspectors entered an examining room where a cystoscopy was about to take place, and noticed that a saline bag, which was hanging on a pole, was dated January 19, said Bob Stahl, of the South Dakota Department of Health. The inspectors, who are registered nurses, questioned the clinic staff. The clinic staff said they routinely reused saline bags and tubing, although both are clearly marked "for single use only," Stahl said. "They used the bags and tubing on multiple patients," Stahl said. He said the workers at the clinic told the inspectors they'd been reusing bags and tubing since the clinic opened in 2002. They said they didn't see anything wrong with the practice, Stahl said. "It was their standard operating procedure," Stahl said. "They told the inspectors that this was a common practice all over the country. We disagreed and told them this was not a common practice." He said that the clinic had been inspected seven times since it opened, and no one had noticed that the clinic was reusing equipment. "It was just by chance that this saline bag was hanging there. We run across these things by luck at times," Stahl said. "We're fortunate that the team was able to identify this." Fluids from patients can retreat into saline bags and tubing while the equipment is used, and reusing the tubing or saline bags could put patients at risk for contacting diseases from previous patients. A 1-liter bag of saline and tubing costs about $4, according to Mary Jo Lallis, account manager for PSS World Medical, Inc., a medical supply company. CNN's Greg Morrison and Elizabeth Cohen contributed to this report.

*By [Your Name], CNN-style report*

**SIOUX FALLS, South Dakota** — A South Dakota urology clinic may have exposed thousands of patients to bloodborne infections including hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV after single-use medical supplies used during cystoscopy procedures were reused, health officials said.

The potential exposure involves patients who underwent cystoscopy, a common procedure in which a thin scope is inserted through the urethra to examine the bladder and urinary tract. State health officials said the concern is tied not to the cystoscope itself, which is typically disinfected or sterilized between patients, but to accessories or supplies labeled for one-time use that may have been used on more than one patient.

Patients who may have been affected are being notified and urged to get tested for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, according to health officials. The risk of infection is believed to be low, but officials said testing is recommended out of an abundance of caution.

Bloodborne viruses can spread when contaminated blood or bodily fluids enter another person’s bloodstream. Hepatitis B and C can cause liver inflammation and, in some cases, long-term liver disease. HIV attacks the immune system but can be managed with treatment if detected early.

Health authorities said they are working with the clinic to review infection-control practices and determine the scope of the potential exposure. The clinic has reportedly stopped using the supplies in question and is cooperating with the investigation.

Officials emphasized that patients should not delay testing if they receive a notification letter or believe they may have been affected. Initial testing can identify prior infection, though follow-up testing may be needed because some viruses can take weeks or months to become detectable after exposure.

Anyone with questions is encouraged to contact their health care provider or the South Dakota Department of Health. Patients who develop symptoms such as fever, fatigue, abdominal pain, dark urine, jaundice or unexplained illness should seek medical attention.

“Patient safety is our highest priority,” the clinic’s statement said. “We are working closely with state health officials to review our historical practices and ensure that all current protocols meet or exceed infection-control standards.”

The clinic also said it has “immediately discontinued any practice that could be inconsistent with manufacturer instructions or regulatory guidance.”

State officials said inspectors are reviewing records, interviewing staff and determining whether the clinic followed manufacturers’ instructions for medical devices and supplies. Many disposable products used in medical procedures are labeled “single use,” meaning they are not intended to be cleaned, sterilized or used again.

“Single-use devices are designed with specific safety limitations,” another inspector said. “When those products are reused, there can be no guarantee that they remain sterile or function as intended.”

The Department of Health said patients who may have been affected will receive letters with information about recommended testing, which could include screening for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. Officials emphasized that notification does not mean a patient was infected.

Public health experts say investigations involving possible reuse of medical products often require extensive record reviews, especially when the practices may have occurred over many years.

**Nearly 5,700 Patients Warned of Possible Infectious-Disease Exposure at South Dakota Clinic**

Nearly 5,700 patients who underwent cystoscopy procedures at a South Dakota clinic are being notified that they may have been exposed to infectious diseases after an investigation found that sterile saline bags, tubing and other equipment were reused between patients, health officials said.

The potential exposure involves patients who received cystoscopy care at the clinic over a period under review by state health authorities. Cystoscopy is a common urologic procedure in which a thin scope is inserted through the urethra to examine the bladder and urinary tract. Although the procedure is routinely performed in outpatient settings, strict infection-control protocols require that certain supplies, including sterile fluids and tubing, be used only once or be properly reprocessed according to manufacturer and federal guidelines.

According to officials, the concern arose after it was discovered that sterile saline bags and associated tubing—items intended for single-patient use—may have been used on multiple patients. Investigators also identified concerns involving other cystoscopy-related equipment, prompting the clinic and health authorities to begin notifying affected patients and recommending testing for bloodborne infections.

The South Dakota Department of Health said the risk of infection is believed to be low, but because reuse of medical supplies can create a pathway for transmission, patients are being advised to undergo testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. Those viruses can be spread through contact with contaminated blood or bodily fluids, even when no symptoms are present.

Health officials emphasized that the notification is precautionary and does not mean that any patient has contracted an infection. Still, they said testing is necessary to determine whether transmission occurred and to provide reassurance to patients who may have been affected.

Patients included in the notification group are expected to receive letters with instructions on how to obtain testing and follow-up care. Public health officials urged anyone who receives a notice to read it carefully and contact the listed medical or public health office with questions. Patients who underwent cystoscopy at the clinic but are unsure whether they are included in the affected group are also encouraged to call the clinic or the state health department.

The incident underscores longstanding infection-control rules designed to prevent cross-contamination in medical settings. Sterile saline bags and tubing used during procedures are generally labeled for single use because once they are accessed, they can become contaminated. If reused, even inadvertently, they can expose subsequent patients to pathogens.

Clinic officials have reportedly stopped the practice and are cooperating with state and federal authorities. Corrective steps may include retraining staff, reviewing sterilization and disinfection procedures, removing improperly used supplies, and strengthening oversight to ensure compliance with infection-prevention standards.

State health officials said they are continuing to investigate how long the practice occurred, which patients were affected and whether any infections can be linked to the lapse. They also said they are working with the clinic to make sure patients receive timely testing and appropriate follow-up.

Medical experts say such incidents are rare but serious because they can undermine confidence in routine care. They note that the infections of greatest concern—HIV and hepatitis B and C—can often be detected through blood tests. Hepatitis B is preventable through vaccination, while hepatitis C is curable in most cases with antiviral treatment. HIV is not curable but can be effectively managed with medication.

Patients who may have been exposed should not delay testing, officials said. In some cases, repeat testing may be recommended because certain infections can take time to become detectable after exposure.

No confirmed cases linked to the equipment reuse have been publicly reported. The investigation remains ongoing.
